title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) students, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback or feedback from human tutors. The broader problem motivating the study is the rapid emergence of generative AI in education and the need for evidence about how it can be incorporated ethically and effectively into writing instruction and assessment.

The authors report two longitudinal studies centered on feedback on student writing. In Study 1, a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental design compared AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback on weekly writing assignments. GPT-4 was prompted to provide structured feedback on topic sentence quality, idea development, academic language, transitions, use of sources/evidence, and grammar. The control group met weekly with trained human tutors in 30-minute one-on-one sessions, while the experimental group received individualized GPT-4 feedback by email and revised their drafts accordingly. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI and human feedback over six weeks and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

The population consisted of 91 undergraduate ENL students at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region, all enrolled in an academic reading and writing language course and assessed at CEFR B1 or above. The context was course-based academic writing instruction focused on 300-word paragraphs tied to class readings and topics. Human tutors were trained English language tutors, and AI feedback was produced using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback over the six-week period. Student preferences were nearly evenly split: some valued human tutors for interaction, engagement, and opportunities to ask follow-up questions, while others preferred AI for its clarity, specificity, consistency, and availability. The authors argue that a blended model may be most beneficial, combining the detailed and efficient feedback generation of AI with the interpersonal and dialogic strengths of human tutoring.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a comparison group, repeated measures, pre/post testing, and reported statistics, but it is not an RCT and is conducted in higher education rather than K-12. The methodology is stronger than correlational work, though external validity for the requested K-12 context is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The main academic literacy finding shows no significant advantage of AI-generated feedback over human tutor feedback, with a negligible posttest effect size (d=-0.156). Perception findings are mixed and near evenly split, so overall impact is best characterized as no clear positive impact.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated automated feedback on university ENL students' academic paragraph writing, including comments on topic sentence, idea development, academic language, transitions, source use, and grammar error tables for revision.
Use of ChatGPT/GPT-4 as an AI writing support tool for corrective feedback and essay evaluation in second-language writing.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, a 6-week quasi-experimental repeated-measures comparison found no significant difference in writing improvement between students receiving GPT-4-generated feedback and those receiving human tutor feedback. The group-by-time interaction was not significant (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063), and posttest scores were similar between groups (EG n=23, M=33.37, SD=1.91; CG n=25, M=33.68, SD=2.07; t=-0.539, p=0.591, d=-0.156) on an analytic writing rubric assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence.
finding.measure: Pre/post academic writing test scores on analytic rubric (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence)
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 for interaction; Cohen's d=-0.156 at posttest
finding.std_deviation: EG pre SD=1.301, CG pre SD=1.391, EG post SD=1.908, CG post SD=2.066

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2, student preference between AI-generated and human feedback was nearly evenly split across 6 weeks among ENL learners receiving both forms of feedback (n=43; weekly responses ranged from 32 to 41). Mean ratings for satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference were all above 4 out of 5 for both feedback sources, with slightly higher grand means for human feedback on satisfaction (4.28 vs. 4.26), clarity (4.32 vs. 4.24), helpfulness (4.31 vs. 4.23), and preference (4.20 vs. 4.13), while the forced-choice preference item averaged 1.53 on a 1=human/2=AI scale, indicating a near-even split; qualitative responses suggested human feedback increased engagement while AI feedback was valued for clarity and specificity.
finding.measure: Weekly Likert surveys on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and preference; qualitative preference explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-generated writing feedback can likely be incorporated without reducing learning outcomes and may save educator time by reducing the burden of reviewing and responding to each student's writing, especially in larger classes. However, this efficiency claim was not directly tested with workload or time-use data, so the evidence is inferential rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Author-reported potential for reduced teacher time/workload; no direct workload metric collected
